seoTitle: Incidence rate Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Incidence rate: work out total population at risk from the total number of new cases and the incidence rate. A free health calculator with the formula,…
summary: The Incidence rate calculator turns the total number of new cases, the incidence rate and the population size into total population at risk. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Nothing repaints underneath you: edit a field, press Calculate, and the new answer appears. That is how you find out which input the result is sensitive to.

sections.title: How does the Incidence rate calculator work?
sections.html:
The Incidence rate calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total population at risk in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the I want to calculate for a different population size); then you type in the total number of new cases, the incidence rate (Results) and the population size.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as no and yes. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A number, expressed in people.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Incidence rate calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Total population at risk=total number of new cases × per ÷ incidence rate
Incidence rate=total number of new cases × population size ÷ total population at risk

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — Total number of new cases = 10, Total population at risk = 10000, per set to 100,000 and I want to calculate for a different population size set to No — it reports Incidence rate = 100.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Incidence rate = 100 should be roughly the size you expected from Total number of new cases = 10 and Total population at risk = 10000.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Incidence rate calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the total number of new cases, the incidence rate and the population size — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Incidence rate calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total population at risk, derived from the total number of new cases, the incidence rate and the population size. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Incidence rate calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the total number of new cases, the incidence rate and the population size, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Incidence rate = 100. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Incidence rate calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
